content: This condition can be asymptomatic or present with symptoms such as lightheadedness, dizziness, blurred vision, or cognitive impairment. It can have either acute or chronic causes, and its management can be particularly challenging in patients who also experience supine hypertension. Orthostatic hypotension can be classified into several subtypes based on the underlying pathophysiology: 1. Initial Orthostatic Hypotension (iOH): This is most commonly observed in healthy adolescents.g., dizziness) within 5 to 15 seconds of standing. Symptoms typically resolve within 20 seconds. 2. Neurogenic Orthostatic Hypotension (nOH): 3. Delayed Orthostatic Hypotension (dOH): This subtype meets the criteria for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension but occurs after three minutes of standing. 4. Neurally Mediated Syncope (vOH): Also known as vasovagal or vasodepressor syncope, this involves a sudden withdrawal of sympathetic vasopressor tone, often during prolonged standing, in individuals with an otherwise intact autonomic nervous system. 5. Cardiovascular Orthostatic Hypotension (cOH): This results from intravascular volume depletion or reduced cardiac output, often accompanied by compensatory tachycardia. 6. Orthostatic Pseudohypotension (pOH): The pathophysiology of orthostatic hypotension involves the pooling of 500 to 1000 mL of blood in the lower extremities and splanchnic circulation upon standing. Disruption of this pathway, due to conditions such as autonomic dysfunction, volume depletion, or medication side effects, can result in orthostatic hypotension and symptoms of cerebral hypoperfusion, including dizziness, nausea, headache, blurred vision, and cognitive impairment. Common causes of orthostatic hypotension include autonomic neuropathies (e.g., Parkinson’s disease, diabetes), volume depletion, prolonged bed rest, and the use of certain medications. It is important to differentiate orthostatic hypotension from other conditions such as neurogenic syncope, cardiogenic syncope, postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), and vasovagal syncope. Orthostatic hypotension is more prevalent in older adults, with its incidence increasing with age. It affects approximately 5% of individuals aged 70 and older and up to 20% of those over 65. Both men and women are equally affected. Risk factors include advanced age, certain medications, autonomic neuropathies, volume depletion, postpartum status, and prolonged bed rest. The natural history of orthostatic hypotension often begins with nonspecific symptoms such as dizziness, lightheadedness, or syncope, particularly in older adults. Complications include an increased risk of falls, cardiovascular events, cognitive decline, and reduced quality of life. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause. A drop of at least 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic confirms the diagnosis. Additional tests, such as blood work, ECG, echocardiography, or imaging studies, may help identify underlying causes. Treatment focuses on symptom management, fall prevention, and addressing supine hypertension.g., heat, alcohol), and consuming smaller, more frequent meals to prevent postprandial hypotension. Pharmacological options include fludrocortisone, midodrine, droxidopa, and pyridostigmine. Secondand third-line therapies may involve erythropoietin, caffeine, yohimbine, or vasopressin analogs. Primary prevention strategies include the ABCDEF method: A: Abdominal compression with a binder. B: Bolus of water and elevating the head of the bed. C: Counter-maneuvers like contracting lower abdominal muscles. D: E: Education and exercise to recognize and manage symptoms. F: Fluids to maintain hydration. Management should be tailored to the individual, with a focus on improving quality of life and minimizing complications.
